```{r}
#| label: page-numbers
#| include: false
# The numbers quoted in the prose, computed when the page is rendered: the
# shares and gaps from the file that the blocks of the page read in the
# browser, with the same reader, and the figures of section 18 from the curve
# of the Housing case study, read from the copy of that site beside this one.
housing <- read.csv("data/housing_emails.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))

n_emails <- format(nrow(housing), big.mark = ",")

# The share greeted by name among the coded replies of each group, and the gaps
# between groups in percentage points, with a typographic minus for the prose
shares <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
share  <- setNames(shares$share, shares$group)
sh     <- setNames(sprintf("%.2f", shares$share), shares$group)
gap_hw <- sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (share[["hispanic"]] - share[["white"]])))
gap_bw <- sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (share[["black"]] - share[["white"]])))
gap_hb <- sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (share[["hispanic"]] - share[["black"]])))

# The curve of the claim as committed on the Housing site; its reference
# specification must give the gap that greeting_gap() computes on this page
curve    <- readr::read_csv("../../ar4ds-housing/data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
n_curve  <- nrow(curve)
ref_spec <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
stopifnot(abs(ref_spec$b_pp - 100 * (share[["hispanic"]] - share[["white"]])) < 1e-9)

# The logit of the reference comparison: its z, converted by the rule of the
# robustness study (the r stored in the curve) and by effectsize::z_to_r()
logit_ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, comparison == "white", population == "replies",
                                     uncoded == "drop", model == "logit", adjust == "none")
z_logit   <- sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", logit_ref$stat))
r_study   <- sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.3f", logit_ref$r))
r_package <- sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.3f", effectsize::z_to_r(logit_ref$stat, logit_ref$n, ci = NULL)$r))
n_logit   <- logit_ref$n
```

This page continues [Getting started with R](r.qmd) and its [second part](r-further.qmd). It stays with the data of the Housing and racial bias case study, the `r n_emails` emails that the original authors (OAs) of a field experiment sent to public housing authorities in the United States [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], and it turns from the functions that come with R and its packages to functions that you write yourself. [Section 16](#sec-functions) builds a first function from the share and the difference in shares of section 10, [section 17](#sec-defaults) gives it defaults and checks and runs it over the groups of names, and [section 18](#sec-helpers) reads, as the same parts on a larger scale, the helper functions with which the exercise of the case study fits its specifications.

The blocks work as they do in the first two parts, as the [note on the code blocks](r.qmd#code-blocks) describes. Run Code runs a whole block, each block holds one step, and the blocks are meant to be run in order. Order matters more on this page than on the other two, since a function defined in one block is called in the blocks after it and defined again, under the same name, as each section adds to it. The page downloads two packages, datawizard and purrr, and again nothing has to be installed on your machine. The sections continue the numbering of the first two parts, so that a reference to section 10 means the section of the first part.

Run the block below first. It reads the data as section 6 of the first part did, and every later block on the page works from the object `housing` that it makes.

```{webr}
housing <- read.csv("data/housing_emails.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

## 16. A function of your own {#sec-functions}

Section 10 computed the gap between the shares of the replies to Hispanic and to white names that greeted the sender by name, and its first exercise computed the gap for the Black names with a copy of the same chain in which the group had changed. Copying code each time that one value changes is how errors enter an analysis, since a later correction reaches some of the copies and misses others. A **function** of your own holds the steps once, under a name of your choosing, as the functions of R and of its packages hold theirs, and it receives the value that changes as an **argument**, so that every comparison runs the same code. This section builds one in three steps: code that works for one comparison, the same code inside a function, and calls that check the function against gaps that you already know.

The first step is code that works for one comparison. The block below keeps the replies that carry a greeting code, as section 10 did, but summarises all three groups of names at once and stores the result as `shares`.

```{webr}
shares <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")

shares
```

The shares are those of section 10 and of its exercise, `r sh[["white"]]` for the white names, `r sh[["black"]]` for the Black names and `r sh[["hispanic"]]` for the Hispanic names, since the share of a group depends only on the replies to that group. Section 10 took the difference between two shares inside `data_summary()`, while here the two shares are taken out of the table with the `$` sign of section 4 and the square brackets of section 3. `shares$share` is the column of shares as a vector, and a condition inside square brackets keeps the values for which the condition is `TRUE`, so `shares$share[shares$group == "hispanic"]` is the share of the Hispanic names. The difference between the two shares, multiplied by 100, is the gap in percentage points.

```{webr}
100 * (shares$share[shares$group == "hispanic"] -
       shares$share[shares$group == "white"])
```

R prints the gap of section 10, `r gap_hw` points once rounded. Of everything in the two blocks, only `"hispanic"`, the group compared with the white names, changes from one comparison to the next, and that value becomes the argument of the function.

The second step puts the same code inside a function. `function()` makes a function, which the arrow stores under a name, here `greeting_gap`, like any other object. The names inside the round brackets are the arguments, the inputs that a call supplies, and the code inside the curly braces is the **body**, which runs whenever the function is called, with each argument standing for the value that the call gave it. The function below has two arguments, `data`, the data frame to summarise, and `compared`, the group of names to compare with the white names. Running the block prints nothing, because the arrow stores the function without calling it.

```{webr}
greeting_gap <- function(data, compared) {
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -
         shares$share[shares$group == "white"])
}
```

The body is the code of the first two blocks of this section with two changes. `housing` became the argument `data`, so that the function summarises whatever data frame it is given, and `"hispanic"` became the argument `compared`. The value that a function hands back to the code that called it is its **return value**, which in R is the value of the last expression in the body, here the arithmetic that gives the gap. A call of `return()` inside the body hands a value back before the last expression is reached, a form that the course seldom needs. The `shares` made inside the body exists only while the function runs, and it is a different object from the `shares` stored in the session by the first block, an object that the function neither reads nor changes.

The third step calls the function and checks it against a value that you know. Called with the Hispanic names, it should return the gap computed above from `shares`.

```{webr}
greeting_gap(housing, "hispanic")
```

The answer is the same, and with the Black names the same function gives the gap of the exercise of section 10, from a change of argument instead of a copy of the chain.

```{webr}
greeting_gap(housing, "black")
```

The exercise found the same gap, `r gap_bw` points. The data come first among the arguments, as in the datawizard verbs, so the function also works at the end of a pipe, and `housing |> greeting_gap("black")` gives the same answer.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Arguments inside the datawizard verbs

The argument `compared` appears only in the arithmetic at the end of the body, outside the datawizard verbs, for a reason that applies to every function written with these verbs. When an expression inside `data_summary()` or `data_modify()` names something that is not a column of the data, datawizard looks the name up among the objects of the session, and never among the arguments of the function from which the verb is called, and `data_filter()` did the same in versions of datawizard before 1.5.0. In those versions a condition such as `group == compared` in `data_filter()` would therefore stop the function with the error `Variable "compared" was not found in the dataset`, or, if the session happened to hold an object called `compared`, would use that object without a warning and return the gap of the wrong group. Inside a function, give the datawizard verbs only columns and fixed values such as `"white"`, as this body does, and take whatever depends on an argument out of the result of the verbs. The helpers of the course choose their rows with dplyr for this reason, as [section 18](#sec-fit-spec) shows.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

The function compares every group with the white names, because `"white"` is written into its body. Fill the blank so that a third argument, `reference`, names the group with which `compared` is compared. The block defines the function and then calls it, comparing the Hispanic with the Black names.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: gap-reference
#| envir: global
greeting_gap <- function(data, compared, reference) {
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -
         shares$share[shares$group == ______])
}

greeting_gap(housing, "hispanic", "black")
```

:::: {.hint exercise="gap-reference"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The blank takes the place of `"white"` in the function above. It holds the name of the new argument, without quotes, since the argument stands for whatever group a call gives it.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="gap-reference"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
greeting_gap <- function(data, compared, reference) {
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -
         shares$share[shares$group == reference])
}

greeting_gap(housing, "hispanic", "black")
```

The gap is `r gap_hb` points, so the share of the replies to the Hispanic names that greeted the sender by name lies below the share among the replies to the Black names, as it lies below the share among the replies to the white names. The call matches its values to the arguments by position, `"hispanic"` to `compared` and `"black"` to `reference`, in the order in which `function()` lists the arguments.
:::
::::

## 17. Defaults, checks and iteration {#sec-defaults}

Most calls of `greeting_gap()` will compare the Hispanic with the white names, the comparison of the claim. An argument can carry a **default**, written with `=` inside the brackets of `function()`, and the function uses the default whenever a call leaves the argument out. The block below gives `compared` the default `"hispanic"` and `reference` the default `"white"`, and the body of the function is that of the exercise above.

```{webr}
greeting_gap <- function(data, compared = "hispanic", reference = "white") {
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -
         shares$share[shares$group == reference])
}
```

Called with the data alone, the function gives the gap of the claim.

```{webr}
greeting_gap(housing)
```

Naming an argument in a call, as in `reference = "black"`, lets the call skip the arguments listed before it and tells a reader which value goes where. The block below keeps the default of `compared` and gives `reference` by name, for the gap of the exercise above.

```{webr}
greeting_gap(housing, reference = "black")
```

A function should also fail in a way that you notice. The column `group` spells the groups in lower case, so a call that writes the Hispanic names with a capital H asks for a group that the data do not hold.

```{webr}
greeting_gap(housing, "Hispanic")
```

R prints `numeric(0)`, a vector of numbers with nothing in it, and no error. The square brackets found no row of `shares` whose group is `"Hispanic"` and picked out nothing, and arithmetic on nothing returns nothing, an empty answer that is easy to miss in a script and that would pass without complaint into a table or a figure. A **check** at the top of the body stops the function with a message instead. `if ()` runs the code inside its braces only when the condition in its brackets is `TRUE`, and `stop()` ends the call with an error whose message is the text of its arguments pasted together. The condition `!compared %in% data$group` is `TRUE` when the value of `compared` is not one of the groups in the data, and `call. = FALSE` leaves the call itself out of the message, so that the message reads as a sentence.

```{webr}
greeting_gap <- function(data, compared = "hispanic", reference = "white") {
  if (!compared %in% data$group) {
    stop("No group of names is called '", compared, "'.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -
         shares$share[shares$group == reference])
}
```

The same call now stops and says why.

```{webr}
greeting_gap(housing, "Hispanic")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

The check covers `compared` only, so a misspelt `reference` still returns `numeric(0)`. Fill the blank so that a second check stops the function when `reference` is not one of the groups in the data. The block ends with a call that the new check should stop.
:::

```{webr}

greeting_gap <- function(data, compared = "hispanic", reference = "white") {

  }
  if (!______ %in% data$group) {
    stop("No group of names is called '", reference, "'.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -

}

greeting_gap(housing, reference = "White")
```

:::: {.hint exercise="check-reference"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The second check repeats the first, with the argument that it checks in place of `compared`.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="check-reference"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
greeting_gap <- function(data, compared = "hispanic", reference = "white") {
  if (!compared %in% data$group) {
    stop("No group of names is called '", compared, "'.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (!reference %in% data$group) {
    stop("No group of names is called '", reference, "'.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  shares <- data |>
    datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
    datawizard::data_summary(share = mean(named), by = "group")
  100 * (shares$share[shares$group == compared] -
         shares$share[shares$group == reference])
}

greeting_gap(housing, reference = "White")
```

The call stops with the message `No group of names is called 'White'.` A check of every argument at the top of the body, before any work is done, is also how the helpers of the course begin, as [section 18](#sec-fit-spec) shows.
:::
::::

A function pays off most when it runs many times. The gaps of the three groups against the white names take three calls, and `map()` from the purrr package makes the calls for you. `map()` takes a vector and a function, calls the function once for each value of the vector, with that value as its first argument, and collects the answers. The function handed to `map()` is usually written on the spot as an **anonymous function**, a function without a name. `\(g) greeting_gap(housing, g)` is a function with one argument, `g`, whose body calls `greeting_gap()` with the data and the group. The name `g` counts only inside the anonymous function, and `\()` is a short way of writing `function()`.

```{webr}
purrr::map(c("white", "black", "hispanic"), \(g) greeting_gap(housing, g))
```

`map()` returns a **list**, a container that can hold a value of any kind in each of its places, here one number for each group, printed under its position in double square brackets. The gap of the white names against themselves is 0, a small check that the function does what it should. When each call returns a single number, `map_dbl()` returns the answers as a vector of numbers instead, its suffix standing for 'double', the type of R for numbers with decimals, and `set_names()`, also from purrr, first names each value of a vector of text after itself, so that every gap carries the name of its group.

```{webr}
c("white", "black", "hispanic") |>
  purrr::set_names() |>
  purrr::map_dbl(\(g) greeting_gap(housing, g))
```

The gaps of section 10 and of its exercise now come from one function and one call, with the gap of 0 for the white names as a check on the function.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Fill the blank so that `map_dbl()` keeps the default of `compared`, the Hispanic names, and passes each group in turn to `reference`, for a comparison of the Hispanic names with the white and then with the Black names.
:::

```{webr}

#| envir: global

```

:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}

``` r
c("white", "black") |>
  purrr::set_names() |>
  purrr::map_dbl(\(r) greeting_gap(housing, reference = r))
```

The two gaps are `r gap_hw` and `r gap_hb` points, the gap of the claim and the gap of the exercise of section 16.
:::
::::

## 18. The helpers of the course {#sec-helpers}

The exercise of the Housing case study fits its specifications with helper functions built from the parts of sections 16 and 17. A **specification** is one complete set of choices for an analysis: which names are compared, which emails are counted, what happens to the uncoded replies, which model is fitted and which covariates it holds. The [specification menu](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/menu.html) of the case study lists every decision and its options. The estimator, `fit_spec()` with the smaller functions that it calls, is written once, in the file `R/_tools.R` of the Housing site, and the scripts of that site build the [specification curve](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/curve.html) of the claim with it. The downloadable workspace of the case study holds a verbatim copy in `R/spec_tools.R`, with the functions that participants call, `try_spec()` among them, and the [browser lab](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/lab.html) holds the same code.

The [page on the helpers of the workspace](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/helpers.html) on the Housing site shows how `try_spec()` is called and what it prints, and this section reads how `fit_spec()`, `try_spec()` and `r_robustness()` are built. The code below is quoted from the two files and is not run on this page, with a line `# ...` in place of each passage left out, and the whole of `R/spec_tools.R` is in the workspace, which the Housing site offers [for download](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/tracks/day/before.html#the-workspace).

### `fit_spec()` {#sec-fit-spec}

`fit_spec()` fits one specification and returns its result, and it reads as follows in `R/_tools.R`.

``` r
fit_spec <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none") {
  check_spec(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
  terms <- ADJUST_TERMS[[adjust]]
  # only the model columns, and only the emails with every covariate;
  # marginaleffects refuses a data column called `group`
  frame <- spec_frame(housing, comparison, population, uncoded) |>
    dplyr::select("y", "hisp", dplyr::all_of(terms)) |>
    stats::na.omit()
  form <- stats::reformulate(c("hisp", terms), response = "y")

  if (model == "lpm") {
    fit <- stats::lm(form, data = frame)
    # HC2 errors (MacKinnon and White 1985) from sandwich::vcovHC() (Zeileis
    # 2004, Journal of Statistical Software), with the t test on the residual df
    coefs <- parameters::model_parameters(fit, vcov = "HC2")
    row <- datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")
    test <- list(coef = row$Coefficient, coef_se = row$SE, stat_type = "t", stat = row$t,
                 df = row$df_error, p = row$p)
    est <- list(b = row$Coefficient, se = row$SE, low = row$CI_low, high = row$CI_high)
  } else {
    fit <- stats::glm(form, family = stats::binomial(), data = frame)
    # ...
    # The average marginal effect: the mean over the analysed emails of the
    # predicted probability with a Hispanic name minus that with a comparison
    # name, with delta-method errors (marginaleffects; Arel-Bundock, Greifer and
    # Heiss 2024, Journal of Statistical Software)
    ame <- marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))
    est <- list(b = ame$estimate, se = ame$std.error, low = ame$conf.low, high = ame$conf.high)
  }

  tibble::tibble(
    comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
    model = model, adjust = adjust,
    b_pp = 100 * est$b, se_pp = 100 * est$se,
    coef = test$coef, coef_se = test$coef_se,
    stat_type = test$stat_type, stat = test$stat, df = test$df, p = test$p,
    r = r_robustness(test$stat, test$stat_type, test$df, nrow(frame)),
    # ...
  )
}
```

Read from the top, the function has the parts of `greeting_gap()`. Its arguments are the data, under the name `housing`, and the five decisions of the menu on which the curve keeps more than one option, each with the option of the reference specification as its default, so that `fit_spec(housing)` estimates the comparison of section 10. Its first line is a check, `check_spec()`, which stops the call before any work is done if an option is not on the curve. The body then builds the analysed rows with `spec_frame()`, looks up the covariates of the chosen adjustment set in the list `ADJUST_TERMS`, defined at the top of the file, turns those covariates into a model formula with `reformulate()`, and fits one of two models, chosen by `if` and `else`. The linear model regresses the greeting on `hisp`, an indicator of the Hispanic names, whose coefficient is the difference in shares, as in section 15, and the other model is a logistic regression, the model of the paper. The return value is the last expression of the body, a table of one row with the decisions, the estimate in percentage points and its standard error, the test of the model and the partial correlation by the rule of the robustness study of SCORE [Multi100\; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]. For the reference specification the estimate is `r gap_hw` points, the gap that `greeting_gap(housing)` returns.

`check_spec()` is the check of section 17 written for five arguments at once.

``` r
check_spec <- function(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust) {
  chosen <- list(comparison = comparison, population = population, uncoded = uncoded,
                 model = model, adjust = adjust)
  bad <- names(chosen)[!purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, SPEC_AXES[names(chosen)], \(v, ok) v %in% ok)]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("Not on the curve: ", paste0(bad, " = '", unlist(chosen[bad]), "'", collapse = ", "),
         ". The options are listed in data/menu_options.csv.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  invisible(TRUE)
}
```

`chosen` is a list of the options of the call, one for each decision, and `SPEC_AXES`, defined at the top of the file, is a list of the options that the curve keeps for each decision. `map2_lgl()` maps over the two lists in parallel, here with an anonymous function of two arguments, `\(v, ok) v %in% ok`, which asks of each decision whether the chosen option is among the options that the curve keeps, and the suffix `lgl` marks answers that come back as logical values, `TRUE` or `FALSE`. The names of the decisions whose answer is `FALSE` are kept in `bad`, and if `bad` holds any name, `stop()` lists each with the option asked for. A check that passes returns `TRUE` through `invisible()`, which hands a value back without printing it, since no call needs to read the value.

The block below sets out a call of `greeting_gap()` in the form that `check_spec()` reads, with the value of each argument in the list `chosen` and the groups allowed for each argument in the list `allowed`, both made by hand with `list()`.

```{webr}
chosen  <- list(compared = "hispanic", reference = "White")
allowed <- list(compared = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                reference = c("white", "black", "hispanic"))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Fill the blank so that `map2_lgl()` asks of each argument what the anonymous function of `check_spec()` asks of each decision, and find the argument that the check would refuse.
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: check-miniature
#| envir: global
purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, allowed, \(v, ok) v %in% ______)
```

:::: {.hint exercise="check-miniature"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The anonymous function receives the chosen value as `v` and the allowed values as `ok`, and `%in%` asks whether the value on its left is one of the values on its right.
:::
::::

:::: {.solution exercise="check-miniature"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

``` r
purrr::map2_lgl(chosen, allowed, \(v, ok) v %in% ok)
```

The answer is `TRUE` for `compared` and `FALSE` for `reference`, because `"White"` is not written as the column `group` spells the groups. `check_spec()` would keep the name `reference` in `bad` and stop with it.
:::
::::

The analysed rows come from `spec_frame()`, which begins as follows in the same file.

``` r
spec_frame <- function(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop") {
  housing |>
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply),
                  .env$comparison == "nonhispanic" | group %in% c("white", "hispanic"),
                  .env$population == "all" | reply == 1) |>
    # ...
}
```

The conditions of `dplyr::filter()` name two arguments of the function, `comparison` and `population`, which `data_filter()` finds only from datawizard 1.5.0, as the note in section 16 warns. The passage left out builds the outcome with `dplyr::mutate()`, where a third argument, `uncoded`, decides what happens to the uncoded replies, and `data_modify()` would not find that argument. The verbs of dplyr look a name up among the columns of the data first and then among the arguments of the function, and `.env$comparison` names the argument explicitly, so that a column called `comparison`, if the data had one, could not take its place. The comment at the head of the file gives the reason: "The rows and the outcome are built with dplyr, because inside a function `datawizard::data_modify()` and `data_summary()` do not find the arguments of that function, and `data_filter()` finds such arguments only from datawizard 1.5.0." `fit_spec()` keeps datawizard where a condition names only a column and a fixed value, as in `datawizard::data_filter(coefs, Parameter == "hisp")`, which picks the row of the indicator out of the table of coefficients.

Every estimate and standard error in the body of `fit_spec()` comes from a package. The HC2 standard errors of the linear model, which allow the variance of the 0/1 outcome to differ between the two groups of names, as section 15 described, come from `parameters::model_parameters()`, which computes these errors with the sandwich package. The logistic regression gives its estimate on the scale of percentage points as an average marginal effect, the mean over the analysed emails of the difference between the predicted probability of a greeting by name with a Hispanic name and with a comparison name, and `marginaleffects::avg_comparisons()` computes that average with its standard error. The comments in the code name the papers behind the two calls, and none of these calculations is written out in the helpers. A standard error written by hand can be wrong in ways that no error message reveals, and a reader can find such a fault only by checking the algebra as well as the code. A package that is maintained, described in a methodological paper and used by many researchers has been checked by its authors and users on far more models than one course could try, and its documentation states what it computes. The course checks its own use of the packages as well. The script `R/check_parity.R` of the Housing site fits every specification of the curve again with estimatr for the HC2 standard errors and margins for the average marginal effect, two packages that share none of the code of `fit_spec()`, and stops if any estimate or standard error disagrees.

`fit_spec()` returns a single row so that many calls can be stacked into one table. The script `R/02_spec_curve.R` of the Housing site builds the curve of the claim in these lines.

``` r
curve <- tidyr::expand_grid(!!!SPEC_AXES) |>
  purrr::pmap(\(comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)
              fit_spec(housing, comparison, population, uncoded, model, adjust)) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(spec_id = dplyr::row_number(), .before = 1)
```

`tidyr::expand_grid()` makes a table with one row for every combination of the options of the five decisions, `r n_curve` rows in all, and `!!!` hands each element of the list `SPEC_AXES` to `expand_grid()` as an argument of its own. `purrr::pmap()` is the `map()` of section 17 over the rows of that table, calling `fit_spec()` once for each row through an anonymous function with one argument for each decision. `dplyr::bind_rows()` then stacks the `r n_curve` tables of one row into the curve, and `dplyr::mutate()` numbers the specifications. The block below follows the same plan on a small scale with `map2_dbl()`, which maps over two vectors in parallel, the groups to compare and their reference groups, and calls `greeting_gap()` once for each pair.

```{webr}
purrr::map2_dbl(
  c("black", "hispanic", "hispanic"),
  c("white", "white", "black"),
  \(compared, reference) greeting_gap(housing, compared, reference)
)
```

Each value is one comparison, as each row of the curve is one specification.

### `try_spec()` {#sec-try-spec}

`try_spec()`, the function with which participants explore specifications in Task 4 of the exercise, wraps `fit_spec()` in what a participant needs, and it reads as follows in `R/spec_tools.R`.

``` r
try_spec <- function(comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop",
                     model = "lpm", adjust = "none", outcome = "named", names = "both",
                     officials = "any", bounced = "exclude", inference = "model", scale = "pp") {
  ch <- .validate(list(outcome = outcome, comparison = comparison, population = population,
                       names = names, officials = officials, uncoded = uncoded,
                       bounced = bounced, model = model, adjust = adjust,
                       inference = inference, scale = scale), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  row <- data.frame(ch, b_pp = res$b_pp, ci_low = res$ci_low, ci_high = res$ci_high,
                    stat_type = res$stat_type, stat = res$stat, p = res$p, n = res$n,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", dplyr::bind_rows(.tried$log, row), envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}
```

`try_spec()` takes no data argument, since a smaller helper, `.housing()`, reads `data/housing_emails.csv` from the workspace once and keeps the result, so a call names only decisions. Its eleven arguments are the decisions of the menu, each with the option of the reference specification as its default, so that `try_spec()` with no arguments fits the comparison of section 10. The first five, the decisions on which the curve keeps more than one option, are the arguments of `fit_spec()`, and the other six are fixed on the curve. The check of the function is `.validate()`, which refuses any option that is not on the curve, giving for an option of the menu the reason recorded in `data/menu_options.csv` and the page of the course site that teaches it. The body then calls `.result()`, which fits the specification with `fit_spec()` and places the estimate among the `r n_curve` of the curve, and `.print_result()`, which prints the lines that a participant reads. A name that begins with a dot marks a function meant for use inside the helpers, and `ls()` leaves such names out when it lists the objects of the session.

Two parts of the body do what no function of sections 16 and 17 does. The two calls of `assign()` change something outside the function, writing into `.tried`, a container of objects that the helpers create once and that outlives every call. The first adds the row of results to the log that `my_experiments()` prints, and the second keeps the last specification for `submit_exploration()`, which sends that specification to the class chart. The return value is `invisible(row)`, the row of results handed back without being printed, because the printed lines are the output to read, while `res <- try_spec(model = "logit")` still keeps the row in `res`.

### `r_robustness()` {#sec-r-robustness}

`r_robustness()` converts the test of a specification into a correlation r, the common scale on which the robustness study set the results of its analysts, as the [page on the robustness article](../robustness-article.qmd#sec-scale) explains with the assumptions of the conversion. The function and the comment above it read as follows in `R/_tools.R`.

``` r
# The conversion rules of the robustness study (standard_correlation_coefficient.R in
# github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100): t with its df, which is the rule of
# effectsize::t_to_r(); z with the sample size standing in for the missing df;
# a chi-square read as the square of a z, so it carries no sign.
r_robustness <- function(stat, stat_type, df, n) {
  dplyr::case_when(
    stat_type == "t" ~ effectsize::t_to_r(stat, df, ci = NULL)$r,
    stat_type == "z" ~ tanh(abs(stat) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3))) * sign(stat),
    stat_type == "chi2" ~ tanh(sqrt(abs(stat)) * sqrt(1 / (n - 3)))
  )
}
```

The four arguments are the statistic of the test, its type, its degrees of freedom and the number of analysed rows. The body is a single call of `dplyr::case_when()`, which returns, for each type of statistic, the value of the formula on the right of its `~`. The rule for t calls a package, `effectsize::t_to_r()`, whose formula, $r = t / \sqrt{t^2 + df}$, is the rule for t in the code published by the robustness study. The rules for z and for a chi-square are written out, because they have to be the rules of `standard_correlation_coefficient.R`, the script with which the team of the robustness study converted the results of its analysts, and the two rules repeat the formulas of that script, apart from the sign that the published rule attaches to a chi-square, a statistic that is never negative.

A package does offer a conversion for z, `effectsize::z_to_r()`, but it follows another rule, $r = z / \sqrt{z^2 + n}$. For the logistic regression of the reference comparison, with z = `r z_logit` on `r n_logit` replies, the rule of the robustness study gives r = `r r_study`, and the rule of the package would give `r r_package`. The difference is small, but only the published rule gives the correlations that the robustness study recorded. Applied to the four statistics recorded by the robustness study for the five analysts of the Housing claim, `r_robustness()` returns the four recorded correlations, as the [meta-analysis module](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/companion/meta-analysis.html#sec-scale) of the Housing site shows, and the correlation that each submission sends to the results form of the class lies on the same scale. The helpers write out a statistical formula only where it has to reproduce a rule published by others, and the comment above the function then names the source, the repository of the team of the robustness study.

## Further study {#sec-sources}

Two chapters of "R for Data Science", the free book by the authors of the tidyverse packages, go further than this page: ["Functions"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/functions.html), which includes functions that call the verbs of dplyr, and ["Iteration"](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/iteration.html), which applies one function to many columns or to many files. The Carpentries lesson "Programming with R", licensed CC BY 4.0, treats functions in ["Creating Functions"](https://swcarpentry.github.io/r-novice-inflammation/02-func-R.html). The vignette ["Programming with dplyr"](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/programming.html) explains how the verbs of dplyr look names up among the columns of the data and among the arguments of a function, the behaviour on which `spec_frame()` relies, and the documentation of purrr, at [purrr.tidyverse.org](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/), covers the whole `map()` family.
